title.value: Halting Time is Predictable for Large Models: A Universality Property and Average-case Analysis
title.justification: The title is explicitly mentioned at the beginning of the document, which is a typical placement for the title of a research paper.
title.quote:
Halting Time is Predictable for Large Models:
A Universality Property and Average-case Analysis

analysis.description: This paper investigates the average-case analysis of algorithms as opposed to the traditional worst-case analysis. It introduces the concept of a universality property for the halting time of large models when trained with first-order methods. The study focuses on how the halting time becomes predictable and independent of the probability distribution of inputs for certain large-scale problems, such as random least squares and one-hidden layer neural networks with random weights. The authors provide explicit average-case convergence rates and demonstrate the universality property through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations.

type.justification: The paper largely discusses the theoretical framework for average-case analysis, presents proofs, and explores theoretical properties of first-order methods, particularly the universality property of halting times.
type.quote:
In fact, the halting time exhibits a universality property: it
is independent of the probability distribution. With this barrier for average-case analysis removed, we
provide the first explicit average-case convergence rates showing a tighter complexity not captured by
traditional worst-case analysis.

name.justification: The paper focuses on the average-case analysis of optimization algorithms, contrasting this with traditional worst-case analysis, and applies the findings to specific optimization problems.
name.quote: Yet, average-case analysis is rarely used in op- timization because the complexity of algorithms is assumed to depend on the specific probability dis- tribution of the inputs.

name.justification: The study uses concepts from random matrix theory to analyze the behavior of optimization algorithms, specifically the universality of halting time.
name.quote: We show that almost all instances of high- dimensional data are indistinguishable to first-order algorithms. Particularly, the halting time, i.e. the number of iterations to reach a given accuracy, for any first-order method converges to a deterministic value which is independent of the input distribution (see Figure 1).

name.justification: The paper draws on concepts from numerical linear algebra, like the halting time of algorithms and the spectral properties of matrices.
name.quote: This work is inspired by research in numerical linear algebra that uses random matrix theory to quantify the 'probability of difficulty' and 'typical behavior' of numerical algorithms.

name.justification: Gradient Descent is explicitly mentioned as a method used in the numerical experiments and theoretical analysis to study convergence rates and halting times.
name.quote: Traditional worst-case analysis of optimization al- gorithms provides complexity bounds for any in- put, no matter how unlikely [Nemirovski, 1995, Nes- terov, 2004].
